mainTopic: Consecrating future rent, taking collateral for Temple debts and offerings, and the need for the owner's willingness (רוצה אני)
overview: The amud begins by finishing a ברייתא about a rented house that was consecrated. Step by step, the גמרא shows that the case only works if the owner consecrated the future rent money. That fits רבי מאיר, who holds a person can consecrate a דבר שלא בא לעולם. A new משנה then teaches that בית דין takes collateral from people who owe ערכין, עולות or שלמים, but not from people who owe חטאות or אשמות. The משנה adds that although an offering must be brought willingly, בית דין may pressure a person until he says 'רוצה אני', and the same is true for a גט. רב פפא says the משנה's rule has exceptions: collateral is taken for a נזיר's חטאת, and not for a מצורע's עולה, which holds him back from purity. A ברייתא gives the source for forcing someone until he says 'רוצה אני'. שמואל teaches that an עולה needs the owner's consent even when a friend separated the animal for him. The amud ends as the גמרא begins an objection to שמואל from a ברייתא, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The base line: the resident consecrated the house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from a ברייתא: if the one living in the house consecrated it, he pays the rent to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the person living in the house consecrated it, he pays the rent to the Temple treasury.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ruling about a rented house that was consecrated. It is setting up a line that it will now examine closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two people here: the owner who rents out the house, and the renter who lives in it. Taken simply, the line says the renter made the house holy and now owes his rent to הקדש. The next step will question whether that is even possible.

keyTerms.meaning: Consecrated; declared something holy property
Holy property, belonging to the Temple treasury
The one living in it, meaning the renter
Pays the rent

phrases.english: If the one living in it consecrated it,
he pays the rent to the Temple treasury.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִקְדִּישׁוֹ הַדָּר בּוֹ מַעֲלֶה שָׂכָר לַהֶקְדֵּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening quote of the ruling under discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the house is consecrated, the resident pays his rent to הקדש.

steps.title: A renter cannot consecrate a house he does not own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that only an owner can consecrate, as learned from the פסוק about consecrating 'his house.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The one living in it consecrated it? How can he consecrate it? The Torah says 'When a man consecrates his house,' which teaches that just as his house is in his possession, so too anything he consecrates must be in his possession.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. A renter does not own the house, so how can he make it holy?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'his house,' and from this the גמרא learns that a person can only consecrate what is truly his. A renter only has the right to live there, not ownership. So the simple reading of the ברייתא seems impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳
In his possession or ownership
Just as... so too...: a way of drawing a general rule from a פסוק

phrases.english: The one living in it consecrated it?
How can he consecrate it?
"When a man shall consecrate his house to be holy"
the Merciful One said,
just as his house is in his possession,
so too anything must be in his possession!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the simple reading of the ruling in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the renter consecrated the house
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק 'his house' limits consecrating to things a person owns, and a renter does not own the house.

steps.title: Reread: the owner consecrated it, the renter pays
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: the owner consecrated the house, and the renter pays the rent to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: if the one renting it out consecrated it, the one living in it pays the rent to the Temple treasury.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the line differently. The owner did the consecrating, and the renter is the one who pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words are split into two parts: 'the owner consecrated it' and 'the resident pays the rent.' This removes the ownership problem, since the owner may consecrate his own house.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is saying: rereading a text to fix a problem
The one who rents out the house, meaning the owner

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
If the one renting it out consecrated it,
the one living in it pays the rent to the Temple treasury.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The renter was the one who consecrated the house
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner consecrated it; the renter only pays the rent to הקדש

steps.title: How can the renter live in a holy house?
steps.stepSummary: If the house itself is holy, living in it would be מעילה, misusing holy property.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the owner consecrated it, how can the renter live in it? He is committing מעילה!
steps.whatsHappening: The new reading causes a new problem. If the house is now holy, the renter is using holy property for himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting personal benefit from הקדש is the sin of מעילה. A person living in a holy house benefits from it every day, so the case as described seems to involve an ongoing sin.

keyTerms.meaning: Misusing or benefiting from holy property
Lives in, dwells
Stands, meaning he is in a state of (a violation)

phrases.english: If the one renting it out consecrated it,
how can he live in it?
He is standing in a violation of מעילה!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the new reading given in step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the owner consecrated the house itself
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the house is holy, living in it is personal benefit from הקדש, which is מעילה.

steps.title: Why would the rent go to הקדש at all?
steps.stepSummary: A second problem: once the renter has misused the holy house, the rent would become ordinary, not holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: And also, he pays the rent to the Temple treasury? Since he misused it, the payment goes out to ordinary status!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second problem to the same reading. Even setting aside the sin, the rent should not belong to הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once holy property is misused, what was misused leaves its holiness. So the use of the house he paid for would already be חולין, and there would be no reason for the rent to go to הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore: adding a second objection
Since
Ordinary, not holy

phrases.english: And furthermore, he pays the rent to the Temple treasury?
Since he misused it,
the payment goes out to ordinary status!

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Part of the same קשיא as step 4
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second objection to the reading in step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the rent goes to הקדש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Misused holy property becomes חולין, so the rent would not be holy.

steps.title: Only the future rent was consecrated
steps.stepSummary: The owner did not consecrate the house, only the rent money that would come in.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where he said: 'When its rent comes to me, it shall be consecrated.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers both problems at once. The owner made only the future rent holy, not the house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the house stays ordinary, the renter is not committing מעילה by living there. The rent goes to הקדש because the owner's statement makes the money holy when it arrives.

keyTerms.meaning: When it comes, in the future
It shall become holy

phrases.english: Where he said:
"When its rent comes to me, it shall be consecrated."
phrases.notes: So the house itself stays ordinary; only the rent money becomes holy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two objections of steps 4 and 5
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner consecrated the house itself
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner consecrated only the future rent money, so there is no מעילה and the rent is holy

steps.title: You cannot consecrate something not yet in existence
steps.stepSummary: The rent does not exist yet, and normally a person cannot consecrate a דבר שלא בא לעולם.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a person cannot consecrate something that has not yet come into the world!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 6. The rent money does not exist yet, so how can it be consecrated?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule that you can only consecrate something that already exists. Future rent is not yet in the owner's hands, so his statement seems to have no effect.

keyTerms.meaning: But surely: opens an objection
Something that has not yet come into existence

phrases.english: But a person cannot consecrate
something that has not come into the world!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אֵין אָדָם מַקְדִּישׁ דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the owner consecrated the future rent
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Future rent is a דבר שלא בא לעולם, which normally cannot be consecrated.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב says the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר, who holds one can consecrate a דבר שלא בא לעולם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Whose view is this? It is רבי מאיר, who says a person can consecrate something that has not yet come into the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by naming the תנא behind the ברייתא. רבי מאיר holds that consecrating future things works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule in step 7 is not agreed on by everyone. By placing the ברייתא in line with רבי מאיר, the case of consecrating future rent makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view is this? Identifying the author of a teaching

steps.whatToRemember: The whole case works only because the owner consecrated future rent, and that fits רבי מאיר, who holds a person can consecrate a דבר שלא בא לעולם.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Meir's,
who says: A person can consecrate
something that has not come into the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying the תנא who holds this view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone holds one cannot consecrate a דבר שלא בא לעולם
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows רבי מאיר, who allows it
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that consecrating future rent depends on a debate, so this ruling only holds by רבי מאיר.

steps.title: Second version: is this really רבי מאיר?
steps.stepSummary: In another version, רב פפא asked אביי (or רב מרי בר חמא asked רב חסדא) whether the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב פפא said to אביי, and some say רב מרי בר חמא said to רב חסדא: Like whom is this? Like רבי מאיר, who says a person can consecrate something not yet in the world?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another version of the same idea. Here it is a question: must the ברייתא really follow רבי מאיר?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The content is the same as step 8, but here the student is asking rather than stating. He wants to know whether the ברייתא has to be limited to רבי מאיר's view.

keyTerms.meaning: Like whom? Following whose opinion?

phrases.english: Some say:
Rav Pappa said to Abaye,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב מָרִי בַּר חָמָא לְרַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: and some say Rav Mari bar Chama said to Rav Chisda:
Like whom? Like Rabbi Meir,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אָדָם מַקְדִּישׁ דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לָעוֹלָם?
phrases.english: who says a person can consecrate something that has not come into the world?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of step 8's answer, phrased as a question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ברייתא must follow רבי מאיר's view

steps.title: Yes, who else could it be?
steps.stepSummary: The teacher answers that of course it follows רבי מאיר, since no other view fits.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Rather, like whom else?!
steps.whatsHappening: The teacher confirms the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר. The answer is a rhetorical question meaning 'it can only be him.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since only רבי מאיר allows consecrating something not yet in existence, the ברייתא can only follow him. Both versions end up with the same result.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, like whom else? Meaning: obviously this view

steps.whatToRemember: Both versions agree: the ruling that the rent goes to הקדש follows רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Rather, like whom else?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, the ברייתא can only follow רבי מאיר

steps.title: Who has collateral taken for what they owe the Temple
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that collateral is taken from people who owe ערכין, עולות and שלמים, but not from people who owe חטאות and אשמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone owes a ערך, we take collateral from him. If someone owes a חטאת or an אשם, we do not take collateral. If someone owes an עולה or a שלמים, we do take collateral.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sorts debts to the Temple into those that בית דין collects by force and those it does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three groups. For ערכין and for עולות and שלמים, בית דין takes collateral. For חטאות and אשמות it does not. The משנה itself gives no reason, but these two offerings come to bring atonement, so the owner is expected to bring them on his own.

keyTerms.meaning: We take collateral (a pledge) from his property to make sure he pays
People who owe a ערך, the fixed 'value' of a person pledged to the Temple
Sin offerings and guilt offerings, which a person brings to get atonement
Burnt offerings and peace offerings, usually brought because of a vow or as a free-will gift

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think חטאות and אשמות matter less. בית דין leaves them alone because the person is expected to bring them by himself, not because they are less important.

phrases.english: MISHNA
Those obligated to pay valuations: we take collateral from them,

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת — אֵין מְמַשְׁכְּנִין אוֹתָן,
phrases.english: those obligated to bring sin offerings and guilt offerings: we do not take collateral from them,
those obligated to bring burnt offerings and peace offerings: we take collateral from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, after the previous discussion about consecrating rent money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Collateral is taken for ערכין, עולות and שלמים, but not for חטאות and אשמות.

steps.title: Forcing a person until he says 'I want to'
steps.stepSummary: An עולה must be brought willingly, yet בית דין may pressure the owner until he says 'רוצה אני'. The same applies to a husband who must give a גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person only gets atonement through his offering if he brings it willingly, because the פסוק says 'לרצונו'. Even so, we force him until he says 'I want to.' The same is true of a גט: we force the husband until he says 'I want to.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers a question its own ruling raises: how can bringing an offering be forced if it must be done willingly? It says בית דין pressures the person until he himself says he wants to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is that the פסוק 'לרצונו' requires the owner to be willing. The משנה's answer is that pressure which ends with the person saying 'רוצה אני' still counts as willing. It then uses the same principle for גיטין, where the husband's will is also required.

keyTerms.meaning: That he becomes willing, agrees by his own choice
'Of his own will', the words in the פסוק showing an offering must be brought willingly
We force (pressure) him
'I want to', his own declaration that he agrees
Bills of divorce given to women

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the well-known idea that forcing someone until he says 'רוצה אני' still counts as his own free will. The idea is used in practice for a גט.
steps.whatToRemember: Pressure that ends with the person saying 'רוצה אני' counts as willing, both for an עולה and for a גט.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר לוֹ
phrases.english: Even though he does not get atonement
until he is willing,
as it is said: "of his own will,"
we force him until he says: "I want to."
And so too you say about women's bills of divorce,
we force him until he says: "I want to."
phrases.notes: This is the husband, in a case where he is required to divorce his wife.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר לוֹ עַד שֶׁיִּתְרַצֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה and explains how taking collateral for an עולה fits with the need for the owner to be willing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even where willingness is required, בית דין may force a person until he says 'רוצה אני'. This applies to offerings and to גיטין.

steps.title: רב פפא: the משנה's rule has exceptions
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says that sometimes collateral is taken for a חטאת, and sometimes it is not taken for an עולה, the opposite of the משנה's general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Sometimes we do take collateral from people who owe a חטאת. And sometimes we do not take collateral from people who owe an עולה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רב פפא, who says the משנה's rule is not absolute. This sets up his next lines, where he explains each exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said no collateral for a חטאת and yes collateral for an עולה. רב פפא says both rules have exceptions. He does not argue with the משנה; he says it describes the usual case.

keyTerms.meaning: Sometimes, in certain cases

phrases.english: GEMARA
Rav Pappa said:
Sometimes, those obligated to bring sin offerings
we do take collateral from them,
and those obligated to bring burnt offerings, we do not take collateral from them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא פְּעָמִים שֶׁחַיָּיבֵי חַטָּאוֹת מְמַשְׁכְּנִין אוֹתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies the משנה's rule from step 11 by saying it has exceptions in both directions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's rule has exceptions: sometimes collateral is taken for a חטאת, and sometimes it is not taken for an עולה.

steps.title: The first exception: the חטאת of a נזיר
steps.stepSummary: Collateral is taken for a נזיר's חטאת. After one of his three offerings is brought, he can already shave, drink wine and become טמא, so he might not bother bringing the חטאת.
steps.simpleTranslation: We take collateral from people who owe a חטאת in the case of a נזיר's חטאת. This is because the Master taught: 'If he shaved after any one of his three offerings, he has fulfilled his duty. And once the blood of any one of the offerings is sprinkled for him, the נזיר may drink wine and become טמא for the dead.' So he is likely to neglect the חטאת and not bring it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains his first exception, the חטאת of a נזיר. Step 15 gives the exception for the עולה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a person brings his חטאת on his own because he needs it. A נזיר is different: once any one of his three offerings is brought, he gets all his permissions back. Since he no longer needs the חטאת for anything, he might put it off, so בית דין takes collateral.

keyTerms.meaning: The sin offering a נזיר brings at the end of his נזירות
Shaved, the shaving that ends a נזיר's term
Was sprinkled, referring to the blood of the offering on the מזבח
Was negligent, did not take care of his duty

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the reason behind the משנה's rule. Collateral depends on whether the person has his own reason to bring the offering, not on what kind of offering it is.

phrases.english: Those obligated to bring sin offerings, we take collateral from them
in the case of a nazirite's sin offering,
because, since the Master said:
"If he shaved after one of the three of them, he has fulfilled his duty,
phrases.notes: At the end of his term a נזיר brings three offerings: an עולה, a שלמים and a חטאת.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם נִזְרַק עָלָיו אֶחָד מִן הַדָּמִים
phrases.english: and if the blood of one of them was sprinkled for him,
the nazirite is permitted to drink wine
and to become impure from the dead."
So he may be negligent with it and not bring it.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַיָּיבֵי חַטָּאוֹת מְמַשְׁכְּנִין אוֹתָן בְּחַטַּאת נָזִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first half of רב פפא's statement in step 13, using a ברייתא about a נזיר as support.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Collateral is taken for a נזיר's חטאת, because he is fully permitted once any one of his offerings is brought and might neglect the חטאת.

steps.title: No collateral is taken for a new mother's burnt offering
steps.stepSummary: The second half of רב פפא's statement: among people who owe an עולה, בית דין does not take collateral for the עולה of a יולדת.
steps.simpleTranslation: People who owe burnt offerings: we do not take collateral from them in the case of the burnt offering of a woman who gave birth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב פפא's statement. Here is a case where we do NOT take collateral for an עולה, even though the משנה's general rule says we do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally בית דין takes collateral for an עולה, because the owner might not bother to bring it. The assumption here is that a יולדת's עולה holds her back, so she has her own reason to bring it and forcing her is unnecessary. The next step questions why her עולה would hold her back, and step 17 replaces this example with a מצורע.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who gave birth, who must bring a עוֹלָה and a חַטָּאת
The burnt offering a woman brings after giving birth
People who are obligated to bring burnt offerings

phrases.english: Those obligated to bring burnt offerings:
we do not take collateral from them
phrases.notes: This finishes רב פפא's line from before: 'sometimes we don't take collateral for an עולה.'

phrases.english: for the burnt offering of a woman after childbirth.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַיָּיבֵי עוֹלוֹת — אֵין מְמַשְׁכְּנִין אוֹתָן בְּעוֹלַת יוֹלֶדֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב פפא's statement. Step 14 gave the חטאת side, and this gives the עולה side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No collateral is taken for a יולדת's עולה, since she will bring it on her own.

steps.title: Challenge: the verse's order is only for reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a יולדת's עולה would hold her back. Is it because the פסוק lists the עולה first? רבא says that order is only for reading, not for the order of bringing.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? That the verse put her burnt offering first? But רבא said: the verse put it first only for the reading!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the יולדת example. It asks what makes her עולה so necessary, and then knocks down the obvious answer using רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the עולה really had to come before the חטאת, she could not finish without it, so she would surely bring it. But רבא says the verse lists the עולה first only in the reading. In practice the חטאת comes first, so she could bring the חטאת and skip the עולה, and then collateral should be needed.

keyTerms.meaning: The פָּסוּק mentioned it first
The verse put it first only in the reading, not in the order of bringing

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the עולה is unimportant. He is only saying the verse's order does not tell us which קרבן is brought first.

phrases.english: What is the reason? Because the verse put it first?
phrases.notes: ויקרא 12:6 lists her עולה before her חטאת.

phrases.english: But didn't רבא say:
The verse put it first only for its reading!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי נִיהוּ דְּאַקְדְּמַיהּ קְרָא, וְהָאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the example of the יולדת given in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a יולדת's עולה needs no collateral
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The only reason would be that the עולה must come first. רבא says the verse's order is only for reading, so she could skip the עולה.

steps.title: Switch the example to a מצורע's burnt offering
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the example: the case is the עולה of a מצורע. A ברייתא says his עולה holds him back just like his חטאת and אשם do.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is the burnt offering of a מצורע. As a ברייתא teaches: רבי ישמעאל son of רבי יהודה בן ברוקה says: Just as his חטאת and his אשם hold him back, so his עולה holds him back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the יולדת example and replaces it with a מצורע. It brings a ברייתא to show why he would bring his עולה on his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי ישמעאל, a מצורע is not fully finished with his purification until all his offerings are brought, including the עולה. Since he cannot finish without it, he will bring it himself. So there is no need for collateral.

keyTerms.meaning: A person with צָרַעַת, who brings a חַטָּאת, an אָשָׁם and an עוֹלָה when he becomes pure
It holds him back. Without it he is not fully finished
A guilt offering

phrases.english: Rather, it is the burnt offering of a מצורע,
as a ברייתא teaches: רבי ישמעאל, son of
רבי יהודה בן ברוקה, says:
Just as his sin offering and his guilt offering hold him back,
phrases.notes: Hold him back from being fully pure until they are brought.

phrases.english: so too his burnt offering holds him back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 by replacing the example.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the case: a different example of an עולה that needs no collateral
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רב פפא meant the יולדת's עולה.
steps.terutzMaskana: He means the מצורע's עולה, which holds him back from purity, so he will bring it on his own.
steps.whatToRemember: No collateral is taken for an עולה that the owner himself needs in order to finish becoming pure, like a מצורע's עולה according to רבי ישמעאל.

steps.title: Source for forcing someone until he says 'I want to'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's line about atonement needing the owner's will. A ברייתא shows from the פסוקים that בית דין forces him until he says 'רוצה אני'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Even though he does not get atonement until he is willing': the Rabbis taught: 'He shall bring it' teaches that we force him. Could it be against his will? The verse says 'of his own will.' How can both be true? We force him until he says 'I want to.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and brings a ברייתא as its source. The ברייתא shows how two words in the same פסוק fit together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'יקריב אותו' shows that בית דין can force the owner to bring it. 'לרצונו' shows that it must be brought willingly. The ברייתא settles this: we pressure him until he himself agrees and says 'רוצה אני'.

keyTerms.meaning: Gets atonement through the קָרְבָּן
We force him (בֵּית דִּין pressures him)
Against his will
Of his own will
How can both be true? (bringing two ideas together)

steps.whyThisMatters: This same idea, forcing someone until he says 'רוצה אני', is the basis for forcing a husband to give a גט, as the משנה mentioned.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר לוֹ
phrases.english: And even though he does not get atonement
until he is willing,
the Rabbis taught: 'He shall bring it'
teaches that we force him.
Could it be against his will?
The verse says: 'Of his own will.'
How can both be true?
We force him until he says: 'I want to.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר לוֹ עַד שֶׁיִּתְרַצֶּה, תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the collateral discussion and goes back to the משנה's rule in step 12 to give its source.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's rule that בית דין forces the owner until he says 'רוצה אני'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading 'יקריב אותו' and 'לרצונו' in ויקרא 1:3 together
steps.whatToRemember: Forcing and 'willingly' fit together: בית דין pressures him until he himself says 'רוצה אני'.

steps.title: A burnt offering needs the owner's consent
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says an עולה needs the owner's דעת, learned from the word ״לִרְצוֹנוֹ״.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: A burnt offering requires consent, as it says: 'of his will.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement from שמואל: an עולה only works if the owner agrees to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל uses the same word the משנה used, ״לִרְצוֹנוֹ״ (of his will). He says that an עולה requires the דעת of the person it atones for. The next step will ask what this adds.

keyTerms.meaning: Burnt offering, burned completely on the מזבח
Here: consent, the owner's agreement
"Of his will", the word in the פסוק showing the owner must want it

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
A burnt offering requires consent,
phrases.notes: He means the consent of the person the offering atones for.

phrases.english: as it is said: 'of his will.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of step 18, that atonement needs the owner's will, with a statement by שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עולה requires the consent of the one it atones for, based on ״לִרְצוֹנוֹ״.

steps.title: Our משנה already says this
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what שמואל adds, since the משנה already teaches that atonement needs the owner's will, from the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? We already learned: Although he does not get atonement until he agrees, as it says: 'of his will'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל: his rule looks like a repeat of what our משנה already said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already said a person is not מתכפר until he agrees, and it quoted the same word ״לִרְצוֹנוֹ״. So שמואל's statement seems to add nothing. The גמרא expects an אמורא's statement to teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: "What is he teaching us?", a challenge that a statement seems to add nothing new
Gets atonement
Until he agrees or is willing

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
We already learned:
phrases.notes: This refers to our own משנה, the line explained in step 18.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר לוֹ
phrases.english: Although he does not get atonement
until he agrees,
as it is said: 'of his will'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 19 as a repeat of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's statement that an עולה requires דעת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה already teaches the same rule from the same פסוק, so שמואל seems to add nothing.

steps.title: Consent is needed even when a friend separated the animal
steps.stepSummary: שמואל means a case where a friend separated the עולה for him. Even then the owner's consent is needed, because he may not want atonement from something that is not his.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where his friend separated it for him. You might have said: we need consent only when the animal is from his own property, but from his friend's we don't. So he teaches us: sometimes a person is not happy to get atonement with something that is not his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that שמואל is teaching something new: consent is needed even when someone else gave the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think consent matters only when the animal comes from his own property, like when בית דין takes his collateral. If a friend pays, the owner loses nothing, so why would he object? שמואל teaches that consent is still needed, because a person may not want atonement through someone else's property.

keyTerms.meaning: "It is only needed for...", showing a statement is meant for a special case
Separated or set aside an animal as an offering
His friend, another person
"You might have said", introducing a mistaken assumption
He is happy with it or comfortable with it

steps.whatToRemember: Atonement needs the person's own willingness, even when the offering is a gift from someone else, because he may not want atonement through another person's property.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where his friend separated it for him.
You might have said:
when we require consent, that is from his own,
phrases.notes: "From his own" means when the animal comes from his own property.

So he teaches us,
sometimes he is not happy
to get atonement with something that is not his.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 20 by narrowing שמואל's statement to a new case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the statement to a specific case (a friend separated the offering)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Consent is needed only when the animal comes from his own property, not when a friend supplies it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Consent is needed even when a friend supplies the animal, because a person may not want atonement from something that is not his.

steps.title: Objection begins: taking on someone else's offerings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins an objection from a ברייתא about a person who says he will bring another person's חטאת and אשם.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: 'The sin offering and guilt offering of so-and-so are upon me'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge to שמואל from a ברייתא. Only the opening case appears here, and the rest of the ברייתא comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a person who takes on the obligation to bring someone else's חטאת and אשם. The rest of the ברייתא, which comes next, will seem to show that one person can bring offerings for another. That would clash with שמואל's rule that the owner must agree.

keyTerms.meaning: Sin offering
Guilt offering
So-and-so, some person
"Upon me", wording that takes on a commitment

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
'The sin offering and guilt offering of so-and-so are upon me'

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: חַטָּאתוֹ וַאֲשָׁמוֹ שֶׁל פְּלוֹנִי עָלַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against שמואל's rule as explained in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that an offering needs the consent of the one it atones for, even when another person supplies it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא deals with one person taking on another's offerings. Its ruling, which comes next, will be used to challenge the need for the owner's consent.
